question: The Commission proposes to make changes to the maximum permitted weights and dimensions for heavy duty vehicles – a renewed push for the EU-wide admission of longer and/or heavier vehicles (LHVs). The Austrian Federal Chamber of Labour (AK) has published a position paper stating its opposition to the introduction of LHVs across Europe1. 1.

The AK claims that the transport infrastructure in Austria and other Member States is not designed for LHVs. The required structural adaptations (roundabouts, tunnels, rest areas, etc.) would cost billions of euros. How does the Commission propose to cover these additional costs?

Introducing LHVs would favour a shift in freight transport from rail to road, both for financial and logistical reasons. In particular in view of other road traffic rules, how does the Commission justify putting forward a proposal that will encourage freight transport to be made by road rather than rail?
LHVs also increase the risk of serious road accidents, with mountain vehicles weighing up to 40 tonnes. How is this proposal compatible with the Commission’s plan to increase road safety?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.3.2024) The Commission proposal to amend the Weights and Dimensions Directive1 increases the weight and/or length of zero-emission (ZE) heavy-duty vehicles (HDV) which are disadvantaged with reduced payload as compared to diesel HDV. The proposal also extends the existing support in terms of extra weight to all intermodal operations (i.e., to noncontainerised transport).

The proposal maintains the Member States’s prerogative to authorise European Modular Systems (EMS) as well as 44-tonne HDVs and limits the authorisation of the latter in international traffic to 2035, unless they are ZE vehicles. It does not require Member States to authorise these longer or heavier vehicles on their territory.

The extra length granted to heavy-duty zero-emission vehicles (HD ZEV) will not require adaptations to the road infrastructure given that it will not exceed the manoeuvrability requirement nor the current standards for HDV equipped with aerodynamic cabs. Similarly, the proposal will have no impact on the road infrastructure of those Member States which will choose not to authorise EMS or non-ZE 44-tonne HDVs.
More generally, the Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal2 has thoroughly analysed the impacts on infrastructure, modal shift, road safety and the environment.

It shows that the proposal will bring five times higher costs savings to public authorities than the overall costs (the majority of which are infrastructure costs), four times larger shift from road-only to intermodal transport than reverse modal shift and that external costs, including CO2 emission and road accidents, will be reduced for value of EUR 7 billion during the period 2025-2050.
